children: President Trump announced Friday night that he is clawing back $810 million in funding already approved by Congress, again challenging lawmakers' authority over government spending and sparking criticism from both Democrats and Republicans.

The cuts, known as pocket rescissions, were mainly for programs that provide health and education services and support for immigrants, refugees and minority-owned businesses. The biggest tranche targeted was $567 million in Health and Human Services funding for programs for noncitizens.
"President Trump is committed to utilizing all possible tools to cut wasteful and harmful government spending that does not benefit American citizens," the White House said.

Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, called them "illegal actions" on Friday and said it was the latest attempt by the administration "to undermine Congress's Constitutional power of the purse."
Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democratic appropriator, called it "theft from the American people, plain and simple."

Trump used a similar maneuver last year, rescinding more than $4 billion in foreign aid. The move was upheld by the Supreme Court, with the majority saying that the president's authority over foreign affairs played a role in its decision. At the time, the White House said it was the first time a pocket rescission was used in nearly 50 years.

The latest move tests the Impoundment Control Act. Under the 1974 law, the White House can pause spending for 45 days while it asks Congress to pass a measure rescinding the money. If Congress doesn't act in 45 days, the money must be released. By sending the request to Congress shortly before the fiscal year ends Sept. 30, the White House is trying to force the cuts through.

The White House's Office of Management and Budget "intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law," Collins added in her post on X.

Russ Vought, the head of the OMB, has argued that Congress doesn't have full control of the purse when it comes to federal spending. He has said he believes the Impoundment Control Act is unconstitutional.
